sections.text: अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च।
He who is incapable of hatred towards any being, who is kind and compassionate, free from selfishness, without pride, equable in pleasure and in pain, and forgiving,
Always contented, self-centred, self-controlled, resolute, with mind and reason dedicated to Me, such a devotee of Mine is My beloved.
He who does not harm the world, and whom the world cannot harm, who is not carried away by any impulse of joy, anger or fear, such a one is My beloved.

So we had been discussing chapter 12. This is bhakti yoga, the Yoga of devotion. As we had been discussing, the Bhagavad Gita is the science of self-improvement.
We started out with the first section of the Bhagavad Gita to understand who we are, how our body, mind, and intellect function, and how we can perform the most effective actions. That segment ended with meditation. Once you understood what is myself and what is not myself, you have to contemplate on it, meditate on it -- to move this identification from this limited self, which is very natural to us (you consider this is me), to that supreme Me, the self which is all-pervading.
And then we have seen the Lords nature. Once you identify with the self, what is the nature of that self? What do I need to meditate on? So in chapters seven through eleven, we have seen the nature of that self, that all-pervading self, and that segment ended in bhakti yoga, the Yoga of devotion. The identification with that supreme self is devotion to that supreme self.
We have many times discussed this: devotion is love. And divine love is nothing but identification. Identification only comes by finding our common traits, our common ground.
Our common ground with the supreme self is: I want happiness -- unlimited happiness, unlimited existence, and unlimited bliss. This is what Im looking for in my life. Scripture says the only way you can achieve it is once you identify with that self.
So Bhakti Yoga is the yoga of devotion -- how to achieve that identification. We have seen there are two ways of meditating upon the supreme: either with form or without form. And Bhagavan said, with form is easier for one who is associated with the body, one who is more attached to this body, this limited ego.
Its easier to identify with the Lord with the form, whatever form that you and I can assign for our own personal God. And then he says, what is devotion? He said, devotion is the complete surrender of my mind to Him. Right now, my mind is surrendered completely to my ego.
My mind and intellect have identified completely with my ego. And therefore I am one with my ego. My identity is my ego.
And therefore all the limitations of my mind and intellect are now the limitations of myself, as identified with the ego. The sorrows Im experiencing in life, the unhappiness Im experiencing -- these are because of these limitations. My inner self is seeking complete happiness, unending happiness, unbound happiness.
But I am identified with my ego, and therefore the limitations of my mind and intellect are creating unpleasant situations. So to get out of this situation, the only way I can achieve that perfect happiness is by identifying with that supreme self -- the self which is residing in me, residing in you, residing in him, residing in her, and in everything that we perceive, think, and consider as our world. Therefore, Bhagavan in the last seven verses of this chapter, starting from verse 13, enumerates the qualities of a true devotee -- a true Bhakta who has surrendered his or her mind and intellect to the supreme self.
Now the mind and intellect have become instruments of the supreme Self, the Lord we have seen. In the last two verses we discussed -- verses 13 and 14 -- Bhagavan has enumerated 11 qualities of a true devotee: Adveshta Sarvabhutanam, Maitrah, Karuna evacha, Nirmamah, Nirahankara, Samaduhkha-sukhah, Kshami. He hates no creature, he is friendly to all beings, hes compassionate, he has no ego, he has no sense of attachment, he is balanced in pleasure and pain.
Santushtah satatam yogi, yatatma, dridha-nishchayah. He is ever content, steady in meditation about who he is. He is self-controlled and possesses firm conviction, with mind and intellect dedicated to the supreme self.
Bhagavan says, such a person is my Bhakta, and he is dear to me. Continuing the same description of the true devotee, Bhagavan describes in verse 15: Yasmat na udvijate Lokah -- he by whom the world is not agitated. If my presence makes the world around me agitated, then obviously there is something I need to correct in myself.
We have experienced this all the time. Some people can just enter a room and suddenly the room is in a positive, joyful mood. They bring that joy, that enthusiasm, that excitement into the room.
And some people come in and there is gloom and doom. We have experienced this with our day-to-day acquaintances and friends. But most profoundly, we have experienced this in the presence of a Mahatma.
I have experienced this in the presence of a great teacher, where people used to sit for hours, including myself, without doing anything -- just sitting in front of him and watching him. It gives you such peace in your mind that you just dont want to leave. When He would come, all the devotees would get together.
Those who were close to him would get a chance to be with him, just be in his room. And He would be doing whatever he was doing. Hed be watching tennis -- watching tennis after lectures.
Somebody would have taped the Wimbledon matches or whatever tournament, and he would be watching that. And other people would just be watching, feeling peace. In the very early days of my exposure to spirituality, my mentor at the time was a chief architect where I used to work as an intern architect.
After the first year of architecture school, during a vacation, he took me to Sant Mota in Surat. At the time I didnt understand much, but because my chief architect told me I should come with him, I went along. Somebody asked Sant Mota a question: How do we know that a person we are meeting is a true saint? Because he could be a cheat, just putting up a show and deceiving people. And Sant Mota said, there is only one test for it.
If in his presence you feel peace, he is a true sadhu or sanyasi. If in his presence your mind gets agitated, consider that person not a genuine saint. At that age -- I was only about 17 -- I couldnt understand how that could be.
But over the years Ive experienced that in the presence of a Mahatma, peace prevails in your mind. Automatically, he projects his peace into your mind and into everyone around him. So Bhagavan said, Yasmat na udvijate Lokah -- he by whom the world is not agitated.
His presence brings peace and joy to the people around him and the world around him. We have heard that in the presence of Lord Buddha and such Mahatmas, even animals would sit down in front of them and feel peace. Lions and tigers have been calmed by Lord Buddha.
Lokat na udvijate cha yah -- neither does he agitate the world, nor can the world agitate him. So these are the qualities you find in a true devotee of the Lord: in his presence you will experience joy, and the agitation in your mind will not affect him. Sometimes everything is going well at home.
But as soon as I come from my office, I create agitation in the house, because I bring my agitation from the office into the home. And now my household, which was peaceful without me, is agitated because of my presence. Thats why we typically have that threat to our children: Well, you just wait -- dad is coming. That means there will be turmoil and agitation in the house. So you behave and dont add any more agitation to his agitation. We put so much burden on our children to calm down their parents.
Obviously Im joking. So Bhagavan said that my devotee is such a person who brings peace to this world and does not get agitated by this world. Harsha, Amarsha, Bhaya, Udvega Muktah -- free from elation, envy, fear, and anxiety.
Such a person, Bhagavan says, Yah sa cha me priyah -- he is closer to me. This does not mean that Bhagavan is partial to him. Rather, he feels the peace prevailing in the supreme self as his own peace, and therefore he is closer to him.
Continuing in the same vein, the next two verses form the third segment of the qualities of a true devotee: Anapekshah, Shuchih, Dakshah, Udasinah, Gatavyathah. So far in the previous stanzas we have seen about 14 characteristics of a true devotee. In this stanza we see six more.
Anapekshah -- he is free from all wants. He has no expectation from this world. Now these are very difficult concepts for you and me to understand, because we live in a world where expectation, anticipation, and performing to someones expectations are a normal part of our vocabulary -- in the business world, in our regular world.
But what we are talking about here is our internal world. We are not talking about the world outside, where I deal with my peers, my superiors, my enemies, and my competitors. Thats the world my ego has created.
The world we are concerned about is the world of my inner self. For that inner self, there is no real enemy, no real competitor, because the same self which is pervading the entire Jagat is also residing in me. And Im trying to get in contact with that.
Once I am in touch with that, Bhagavan said, you will have no Apeksha. I am satisfied by my own self, and therefore I have no other expectation from the world. Up till now, my expectation was that the world will make me happy.
My children will grow up and do this and that, and they will make me happy. My wife will do this and that will make me happy. My friends will do this and that will make me happy.
I have mortgaged my happiness with all the people I know, but have not left anything for me to do. So now I have no control over my happiness -- I have to rely on the people with whom Ive mortgaged it. They have to do something to make me happy.
My children have to perform well in their studies or in their sports or whatever I expect them to do. My wife has to perform according to my desires. My friends have to behave the way I want.
When they do that, Ill be happy. So I mortgage my happiness. And therefore I have Apeksha -- expectations from the world to make me happy.
Bhagavan says my devotee is Anapekshah. There is no expectation because he is the reservoir of his own happiness. Shuchih -- someone who is devoted to the Lord cannot be filthy and dirty, both in his own mind and intellect, and also in his surroundings.
He will live a clean life, both inside and out. When your mind is clean you automatically will make your environment around you clean. It has a reverse effect also.
When my environment around me is clean it will calm my mind down and my mind will be clean too. Dakshah -- there is no laziness in him.

These verses begin Krishnas portrait of the ideal devotee, and the qualities are striking: Adveshta sarvabhutanam, incapable of hatred toward any being. Not merely controlling hatred, but being constitutionally incapable of it. Maitrah karunah, friendly and compassionate. Nirmamah nirahankarah, free from possessiveness and ego. Samadukhha-sukhah, balanced in pain and pleasure. These are not commandments to follow but descriptions of what naturally emerges when the mind is surrendered to the Divine. The devotee does not struggle to be compassionate; compassion flows naturally when the ego-barrier dissolves.
Verse 15 offers a powerful diagnostic: He who does not harm the world, and whom the world cannot harm (yasmat na udvijate lokah, lokat na udvijate ca yah). The teaching illustrates this beautifully with the example of Sant Motas test for a true sadhu: if you feel peace in someones presence, they are genuine; if you feel agitated, they are not. Consider: What effect does your presence have on others? When you enter a room, does the atmosphere lighten or tense? This is not about being artificially pleasant but about the natural radiation of an untroubled mind.
For todays practice, focus on the quality of kshami, forgiveness. Identify one person toward whom you hold resentment, however small. You need not contact them or resolve the situation externally. Simply sit quietly and consciously release the grip of that resentment. Notice how the mind wants to justify holding on, But they really did wrong me. Acknowledge that and release anyway. True forgiveness is not about condoning actions but about freeing your own mind from the prison of grievance. Observe: Does this release bring any taste of the peace Krishna describes?
